# Mathematical Astronomy

## Why Astronomy Belongs in a Mathematics Reference

In this period astronomy **was** applied mathematics: the zij (astronomical handbook with tables) was the tradition's characteristic mathematical publication, over 200 are known (Kennedy's survey), and the problems of astronomy drove trigonometry, spherical geometry, numerical methods, and instrument theory. Four strands matter most.

## Strand 1: The Zij Tradition

From [al-Khwarizmi](../scholars/era-01-foundations.md#al-khwarizmi)'s *Sindhind* (Indian methods) through [al-Battani](../scholars/era-01-foundations.md#al-battani)'s observation-based *Sabian Tables*, [Ibn Yunus](../scholars/era-02-tenth-century.md#ibn-yunus)'s *Hakimi Zij*, the [Toledan Tables](../scholars/era-03-golden-age.md#ibn-al-samh-and-the-school-of-al-andalus) of al-Zarqali's circle, down to Ulugh Beg's *Zij-i Sultani*, the zij genre packaged theory as computation: mean motions, equations (correction functions), trigonometric tables, geographic coordinates, calendar conversions. Producing one required exactly the skills of a modern scientific-computing team: model selection, parameter fitting to observation, function tabulation, interpolation design, and error control. Europe's Alfonsine Tables (13th c.), its standard until the sixteenth century, are a direct continuation of this genre out of the Toledan material.

## Strand 2: Observation Programs and Instruments

Al-Ma'mun's Baghdad/Damascus observations (9th c.) established the state-funded observational program; [al-Khujandi](../scholars/era-02-tenth-century.md#al-khujandi)'s giant sextant at Rayy, the **Maragha observatory** (1259, the first institution recognizable as a research observatory, with library and staff), and **Samarkand** (c. 1424, with its 40-meter meridian arc) scaled instruments up because accuracy scales with size, the same logic as modern telescope apertures. [Taqi al-Din](../scholars/era-08-later.md#taqi-al-din)'s Istanbul observatory (1577) was the tradition's last great installation, contemporary with Tycho's Uraniborg. Aydin Sayili's *The Observatory in Islam* traces the institutional history; the observatory as an institution is itself an Islamic-civilization invention.

## Strand 3: Criticism of Ptolemy and the Maragha Program

[Ibn al-Haytham](../scholars/era-03-golden-age.md#ibn-al-haytham)'s *Doubts Concerning Ptolemy* indicted the equant and related devices as violations of the uniform-circular-motion physics Ptolemy himself professed. The **Maragha school** answered with new mathematics: the [Tusi couple](../scholars/era-05-maragha.md#nasir-al-din-al-tusi) (two circles producing straight-line oscillation), [Urdi's lemma](../scholars/era-05-maragha.md#al-urdi), and their deployment by Qutb al-Din al-Shirazi and, in perfected form, by [Ibn al-Shatir](../scholars/era-06-fourteenth.md#ibn-al-shatir) of Damascus, whose equant-free lunar and planetary models are mathematically identical to Copernicus's (minus heliocentrism). The transmission question, Byzantine intermediaries, Italian orientalists, the Jewish scholar Moses Galeano's Veneto connections, is one of the most active debates in the history of science; see [Renaissance Connections](../transmission/renaissance-links.md).

## Strand 4: Timekeeping and the Science of the Muwaqqit

Islamic ritual created a permanent institutional demand for spherical astronomy: prayer times defined by solar altitudes, mosque orientation by the qibla, month beginnings by lunar crescent visibility (a genuinely hard problem, still imperfectly modeled today). The professional *muwaqqit* and the *ilm al-miqat* (science of timekeeping) generated the enormous table literature David King has documented, with [al-Khalili](../scholars/era-06-fourteenth.md#al-khalili)'s universal tables as its summit, and kept computational astronomy alive in Cairo and Damascus into the nineteenth century.

## Modern Connections

Star names (Aldebaran, Altair, Betelgeuse, Deneb, Rigel, Vega, dozens more) and terms (zenith, nadir, azimuth, almanac) are Arabic survivals in the modern sky; see [Etymology](../legacy/etymology.md). Medieval Islamic eclipse and occultation records are used in current research on Earth's rotational deceleration (ΔT studies), Ibn Yunus's Cairo records being especially valuable. And the zij is the direct ancestor, through the Alfonsine and Rudolphine tables, of the modern ephemeris, computed today by JPL and used by every spacecraft navigator.

*Sources: E. S. Kennedy, "A Survey of Islamic Astronomical Tables" (1956); D. A. King, In Synchrony with the Heavens (2004–05); Saliba, Islamic Science and the Making of the European Renaissance; A. Sayili, The Observatory in Islam; Swerdlow & Neugebauer.*
